title: The first maor's seal cut from Clàr nan Suaicheantas
summary: The council's clerk Tòmas cuts the first working seal from Clàr nan Suaicheantas, the newly drawn roll of arms, for a maor of the south-west to press upon his letters; the shire's borrowed lion goes out sealing writs before the ink of the roll itself is fully dry.

title: Coinneach mac Ailein settles the fishwives' stall-place
summary: In his first sitting under the market roof at Baile Mòr mhòr, the new maor Coinneach mac Ailein settles a two-year quarrel over a stall-place by asking the gathered stallholders for the truth of it rather than ruling from the bench alone, and takes their answer as his judgment.

title: The council votes a relief party for the southern coast
summary: Before its morning sitting breaks, Comhairle na Rìoghachd votes grain, blankets, timber and men down the coast road to Cuan dhearg, and orders a tally kept of what is found, the first time the twelve have met before full light since An Dealachadh itself.

title: Ailean's tally-book of the wave begun
summary: Ailean mac Iain, sent south with the relief party, opens a plain tally-book at Cuan dhearg and enters the first of what will be a summer's counting: boats found standing in the fields, wells fouled or sweet, dead named where they can be and marked only by place where they cannot.

title: The dead of Cuan dhearg buried on the rise
summary: Through the first fortnight after the wave, the dead of Cuan dhearg are carried up onto the rise above the old harbour line and buried in ground the sea has not reached, while the town's clerks mark by place what names cannot be recovered.

title: The boats left standing in the barley
summary: The wrecked fishing boats of Cuan dhearg, carried inland by the wave and left standing among the barley behind the town, are judged too many to right before winter and are left through the harvest, one still upright in its furrow with its mast stepped.

title: The treasury's first relief roll voted
summary: On the count of a little over forty dead, the council votes seed and removal for the survivors of Achadh mhin out of the treasury without a due asked in return, over one councillor's question of cost, answered that a kingdom that finds silver for a roll of arms can find grain for its own dead.

title: Ros gharbh's fleet counted on the headland
summary: Ailean mac Iain walks the headland above Ros gharbh's harbour and counts the town's fishing fleet where the wave cast it, hull by hull, sound or stove, and carries the count south as proof that a town spared its people can still be ruined in its trade.

title: Ros gharbh's boats rebuilt
summary: Through the following year Ros gharbh borrows hulls from harbours the wave did not reach while shipwrights from beyond the gulf raise its fleet anew on the cleared beach, one keel at a time, until the last boat is launched and the town's people begin calling that whole year simply the bad year.

title: A hill shire questions its new arms
summary: A custodian's widow keeping a south-western shire's books asks the council's clerk whether a shire that never bore a badge under the old custody must bear one now, and is answered that any shire's writs are read faster at Cathair dhearg with a seal, borrowed beast or none, than without one.

title: Coinneach mac Ailein moves his court back under the market roof
summary: When Baile Mòr mhòr's new courthouse is raised at last, Coinneach mac Ailein sits in it for a single sitting and moves his court back under the market roof among the fish-scales the week after; the two maoir after him do the same, and no one writes down why.

title: Tòmas draws Clàr nan Suaicheantas
summary: Tòmas, a mason's clerk before the war and a council clerk since, draws Clàr nan Suaicheantas for the maoir's seals, copying many of its charges from a book of arms left at Taigh an Àrd-mhaoir, so that lions and parrots and crocodiles come to stand on the seals of shires where none was ever seen.
